content_voiceover: This slide drills into model one, the protein antigens. The common pattern is a single nucleotide polymorphism, a SNP, in the gene that produces two allelic forms of the protein, labeled a and b, and these are called antithetical antigens, meaning if you're negative for one you're almost always positive for the other. Kidd blood group, Jk-a and Jk-b, is the textbook example. Now the less common but board-relevant case, especially if you're thinking about Taiwan, is the Mi-a antigen, also called Mur or Mi-three. This arises from a homologous crossover between the glycophorin A and glycophorin B genes, creating a hybrid GP-B-A-B-Mur protein that displays a brand new antigen not present on either parent protein. Here's the number to memorize, about seven point three percent of the Taiwanese population is Mi-a positive, compared to essentially zero in Caucasians, and anti-Mi-a is actually the most common unexpected, irregular antibody found in Taiwan. That combination of high antigen frequency plus ethnic specificity is exactly the kind of fact boards like to test.
keypoints: Antithetical antigens from SNPs, classic example Jk-a slash Jk-b in Kidd system
Mi-a (Mur, Mi-III) arises from GPA-GPB gene crossover, a hybrid glycophorin
Taiwan: ~7.3% Mi-a positive versus near 0% in Caucasians
Anti-Mi-a is the most common irregular antibody in Taiwan
keypoint_voiceover: Two protein antigen concepts to lock in. First, SNP-driven antithetical pairs, like Jk-a and Jk-b in the Kidd system. Second, the Mi-a antigen, also called Mur or Mi-three, which comes from a crossover hybrid of glycophorin A and B genes. The board fact to remember, about seven percent of Taiwanese are Mi-a positive versus almost no Caucasians, and anti-Mi-a is the single most common irregular antibody encountered in Taiwan.
